input.question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?
input.ground_truth: Because over a given part of the earth the wind moves predominantly in one direction . Hence one way the plane is flying into the wind and one it's flying with the wind. At the altitude of airliners the wind speeds constitute a noticeable fraction of the nominal speed of the aircraft - hence the difference. EDIT: I should have added that for this reason I wouldn't expect to see the affect you're describing on a generally north-south routing (eg london - cape town).

Question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the Earth is like a big, slow-moving merry-go-round.

When you fly **East to West**, you're going *against* the way the Earth spins. It's like trying to walk backwards on a moving sidewalk that's going forward. So, the Earth is spinning under you, and you have to cover a little extra distance because the ground is moving the other way. That makes your trip a tiny bit longer.

When you fly **West to East**, you're going *with* the way the Earth spins. It's like walking forward on that same moving sidewalk. The Earth is spinning in the same direction as you, so you kind of get a little "push" from the Earth, and your trip is a tiny bit shorter.

But don't worry, the difference is so small that you probably won't notice it on a normal flight! The Earth just spins a little bit while you're in the air.
